chapter_title: User and Group Management for Security
chapter_summary:
Secure user and group management is a cornerstone of system security, preventing unauthorized access and limiting the blast radius of compromised accounts. A critical first step is establishing strong password policies. The Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) framework is the standard for enforcing these policies on Linux. Specifically, the `pam_pwquality.so` module (or `pam_cracklib.so` on older systems) allows you to define requirements for password length, character complexity (uppercase, lowercase, digits, special characters), and dictionary checks. You configure this in files like `/etc/pam.d/system-auth` or `/etc/pam.d/passwd`. For example, adding `minlen=12 ucredit=-1 lcredit=-1 dcredit=-1 ocredit=-1` to `pam_pwquality.so` enforces a minimum length of 12 characters and requires at least one uppercase, one lowercase, one digit, and one other character. Beyond complexity, password aging is vital. The `chage` command allows administrators to set password expiration dates, minimum days between changes, and warning periods. For example, `chage -M 90 -m 7 -W 14 username` sets a maximum password age of 90 days, a minimum of 7 days before it can be changed again, and warns the user 14 days before expiration. Regularly auditing password ages and ensuring users adhere to policies prevents stale credentials from becoming vulnerabilities.

Privilege escalation is a major security concern, and the `sudo` command is the primary mechanism for granting elevated privileges safely. Instead of sharing the `root` password, `sudo` allows specific users or groups to execute commands as `root` (or another user) with fine-grained control. The `/etc/sudoers` file, edited exclusively with `visudo`, defines these permissions. Best practice dictates granting the *least privilege necessary*. Avoid `ALL=(ALL) ALL` for regular users. Instead, specify exact commands, and even arguments, that a user or group can run. For example, `appadmin ALL=(root) /usr/bin/systemctl restart apache2` allows `appadmin` to restart Apache but nothing else as root. You can also use aliases for commands and hosts to simplify complex `sudoers` files. Crucially, `sudo` logs all executed commands, providing an audit trail. Reviewing `sudo` logs in `/var/log/auth.log` or `journalctl` is essential for monitoring administrative actions and detecting suspicious activity. A common mistake is adding users to the `sudo` or `wheel` group without understanding the implications, effectively giving them full root access without proper oversight. Always specify commands explicitly.

Linux systems also feature several special user accounts that are not intended for interactive login but are crucial for system operation. These include system users (e.g., `daemon`, `bin`, `sys`) and application-specific users (e.g., `nginx`, `mysql`, `apache`). These accounts typically have a shell set to `/sbin/nologin` or `/bin/false` and a password field indicating `*` or `!`, preventing direct login. Understanding the purpose of each system user and ensuring they adhere to the principle of least privilege is vital. For instance, a web server like Nginx should run as a dedicated, unprivileged user (e.g., `nginx`), with its files and directories owned by this user, restricting its access to only what's necessary to serve web content. Never run services as `root` unless absolutely unavoidable, and even then, ensure they drop privileges immediately after startup. Regularly audit `/etc/passwd` and `/etc/shadow` for any unexpected interactive shells or password hashes on system accounts.

Finally, account locking and monitoring for brute-force attempts are essential proactive security measures. PAM can be configured to automatically lock accounts after a certain number of failed login attempts using the `pam_faillock.so` module. In `/etc/pam.d/system-auth` or `/etc/pam.d/sshd`, you might add lines like `auth required pam_faillock.so deny=3 unlock_time=600` to lock an account for 10 minutes after 3 failed attempts. This significantly hinders brute-force attacks against SSH or other services. Tools like `fail2ban` take this a step further by actively parsing log files (e.g., `/var/log/auth.log`) and dynamically updating firewall rules to block IP addresses that exhibit suspicious behavior, such as repeated failed SSH login attempts. Configuring `fail2ban` with appropriate jails for SSH, web servers, and other services is a highly effective way to automate protection against common attack vectors. Regularly review `fail2ban` logs and `faillock` entries to understand the attack landscape and adjust policies as needed.

screens.title: User and Group Management for Security
screens.subtitle: Hardening accounts, enforcing password policy, least-privilege sudo, and automated account locking

narration.text: Secure user and group management reduces attack surface and limits damage when an account is compromised. In this lesson you will learn the practical tools and configurations used on Linux systems to enforce strong passwords, set expiration policies, grant only required privileges via sudo, and automatically lock or block attackers after repeated failures. We'll focus on the PAM framework and its modules for password complexity, the chage utility for password aging, best practices editing the sudoers file with visudo, the role and handling of non-interactive system users, and automated protections such as pam_faillock and fail2ban. Each topic includes a clear configuration example and a short test sequence you can follow in a terminal lab. By the end you will be able to write a pam_pwquality rule for length and character classes, set sensible chage parameters, craft a narrowly scoped sudoers entry, and add a simple faillock or fail2ban rule to block repeated login attempts. As you move through the slides, watch for common mistakes — like adding users to sudo without restrictions or allowing interactive shells for system accounts — and a few quick checks you can run to validate your work.

keyIdea.title: Security by correct account policy
keyIdea.text: Combine PAM rules, password aging, least-privilege sudo, and automated locking to reduce unauthorized access and audit administrative actions.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will implement and verify four core account security skills. First, you will enforce robust password policies using PAM modules that check length, character classes, and dictionary words so that weak credentials are rejected at creation time. Second, you will configure password aging with the chage utility to require regular rotation and present users with timely warnings. Third, you will grant administrative capabilities with sudo using visudo, applying the principle of least privilege and limited command lists for safer escalation. Fourth, you will implement automatic account locking and monitoring so repeated failed authentications are contained and hostile IPs can be blocked. Each objective includes a short validation step: create a test user, attempt a weak password, set password expiry, add a tailored sudoers entry for a single service command, and simulate failed SSH logins to see locking in action. These skills protect credentials, produce audit logs, and reduce the blast radius of a compromised account. A common misconception is that adding someone to the sudo group is equivalent to proper delegation — it is not. Learning to scope sudo rules and monitor failures will make your systems far safer.

keyIdea.title: Practical security milestones
keyIdea.text: You will be able to enforce password quality, age credentials, grant minimal sudo privileges, and activate automated locking and blocking.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Implementation Focus
screens.subtitle: How you will validate each objective in a terminal lab

narration.text: This slide drills into how you will test each objective inside a lab environment. For password policies, you will edit the distribution's PAM password line and then create a new test user and attempt weak and strong passwords to observe rejection messages. For password aging, you will set a maximum age and a warning period and inspect the account's metadata to confirm expiry and warning counters. For sudo, you will create a narrowly scoped sudoers entry with a command alias and test allowed and disallowed commands while checking the sudo log for audit entries. For locking and blocking, you will configure pam_faillock to lock accounts after a few failed attempts and use fail2ban with an SSH jail to demonstrate dynamic blocking; then inspect lock records and jail logs to confirm the behavior. Each validation step shows the expected outcome and a short troubleshooting note so you can tell whether the configuration is active. This makes the objectives concrete: not only will you change files, you will verify, audit, and correct misconfigurations so the settings work as intended.

keyIdea.title: From config to verification
keyIdea.text: Every policy change should include a short validation workflow: attempt, observe, and audit the results.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Learning Objectives — Implementation
Validation checklist
Short terminal checks you will run after each change.
PAM policy check
  • Edit the pam_pwquality line and save with the appropriate tool for your distribution.
  • Create a new user and attempt a weak password; expect a clear rejection message from PAM.
  • Try a compliant password and confirm account creation succeeds.
chage and expiry
  • Set maximum age and warning period for a test user and run the command to view expiry fields.
  • Confirm the warning appears within the configured window when close to expiry.
  • Use account metadata in /etc/shadow to audit real values.
Sudo testing
  • Create a limited sudoers entry with visudo and test an allowed command as the target user.
  • Try a disallowed command and observe the denial and sudo log entry.
  • Review the audit trail in auth logs to ensure visibility of elevated actions.
Locking & fail2ban
  • Configure a faillock rule that locks after a small number of failures and test from a separate client.
  • Enable an SSH jail in fail2ban and generate repeated failures to see a dynamic ban in action.
  • Inspect faillock and fail2ban logs to confirm the block and reset the test user as needed.

screens.title: PAM — The authentication framework
screens.subtitle: What PAM is and why it centralizes authentication policy

narration.text: PAM, the Pluggable Authentication Modules framework, centralizes authentication decisions for services without forcing each program to implement its own checks. Think of PAM as a set of ordered rules that each service consults when a user tries to authenticate. Each rule is a module — for example, one module verifies local password hashes, another consults an external directory, and another enforces password complexity at creation time. That modular approach matters because administrators can change authentication behavior for many services by editing a handful of PAM configuration files rather than touching each program. A practical example is enabling a module that rejects passwords found in a dictionary; once configured, password creation is blocked across logins and password-change tools. A common misconception is that PAM alone enforces password rotation; it does not. PAM evaluates authentication and password quality at the moment of use, while utilities like chage manage aging and expiry metadata. Key checks when working with PAM are the order of lines, which control short-circuit behavior, and ensuring services include the correct pam. d file. To verify, update a PAM password module, create a test user, try weak and strong passwords, and watch the PAM error messages — that feedback shows whether the module is active. Why does this matter? Centralized, modular authentication reduces configuration drift and gives you a single place to raise security standards across the system.

keyIdea.title: PAM centralizes auth
keyIdea.text: Use PAM modules to implement cross-service authentication policies without changing every application.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › PAM — The authentication framework
Definition
PAM is a modular system of authentication modules that services consult to permit or deny access.
Why it matters
Change a single PAM rule and you affect all services that call that PAM stack, enabling consistent enforcement of password quality and account locking.
Common misconception
PAM enforces policy at authentication time but does not manage password expiry metadata; for that you use tools that update account fields such as chage.
Key Takeaway

PAM gives you a single extensible point to enforce authentication rules across services, making policy changes consistent and auditable.

Analogy & example
Imagine PAM as a receptionist with a set of checklists. Each module is one checklist item. If a password fails a quality checklist, the receptionist refuses the request and explains why. The same receptionist serves many offices, so one change affects all visitors.
Quick verification steps
  1. Edit the PAM password line for your distribution (common-password or system-auth).
  2. Create a test user and attempt a weak password to confirm rejection messages.
  3. Try a compliant password to confirm success.
Pro tip
Make backup copies of PAM files before editing and test on a non-production host to avoid locking out administrators unexpectedly.
Check your understanding
What would you change first if a service still accepted weak passwords after a PAM rule change?

screens.title: Configuring pam_pwquality for complexity
screens.subtitle: Example configuration and a lab test sequence

narration.text: The pam_pwquality module enforces complexity and dictionary checks when users set or change passwords. You will add parameters that set a minimum length and require character classes, such as uppercase, lowercase, digits, and special characters. In many distributions this line lives in the file that controls password handling — often common-password or system-auth. A concrete example is adding options that require a minimum length of fourteen characters and at least one character from each class. After making the change, create a test account and attempt to set a weak password; PAM will return an explanatory error telling you which rule failed. A frequent mistake is to forget the enforce_for_root option if you want the same rules applied to the root account. Another is editing the wrong configuration file for your distribution; verify which PAM file the password flow uses by checking your distribution's documentation or the service pam. d include lines. The visible code block on this slide shows a sample pam_pwquality line you can copy into a lab file. Remember to test with both failing and passing passwords to confirm the rule is active. What will you observe when a password fails the dictionary check? You will see a PAM error explaining the dictionary match, which helps refine your configuration.

keyIdea.title: pam_pwquality enforces composition
keyIdea.text: Set minlen and credit values to require specific character classes and block common words across all password changes.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › pam_pwquality configuration
Configuration example
Add or update the password module line with specific options for length and character classes.
# Example pam_pwquality configuration line (place in common-password or system-auth)
password    requisite     pam_pwquality.so retry=3 minlen=14 ucredit=-1 lcredit=-1 dcredit=-1 ocredit=-1 enforce_for_root
Notes
  • minlen sets the shortest allowed password length.
  • ucredit, lcredit, dcredit, and ocredit require character classes by using negative values.
  • retry configures how many times a user may retry during password entry.
Lab test sequence
  1. Create a test account and try to set an intentionally weak password. Expect a PAM rejection with a reason.
  2. Set a compliant password using the required classes and confirm success.
  3. If rejection persists, confirm you edited the correct PAM file and that the service uses that stack.
Common mistake
Editing the wrong PAM file or failing to restart the service that sources a different pam.d entry will make changes appear ineffective.
Key Takeaway

Use pam_pwquality options to set a strict baseline and always validate by creating a test user and trying weak and strong passwords.

screens.title: Password aging with chage
screens.subtitle: Set expiry, minimum change interval, and warnings

narration.text: Password aging prevents credentials from becoming permanent and reduces exposure from long-lived passwords. The chage utility updates account aging metadata such as maximum days until expiry, minimum days between changes, and the warning window before expiry. For example, setting a maximum of ninety days with a fourteen day warning ensures users are prompted in advance to rotate credentials. In practice you pick a maximum that balances security and usability, and you set a minimum to prevent rapid cycling that could subvert password history policies. The visible code panel contains concrete chage examples you can run in a lab. After applying chage to a test user, inspect the account fields to confirm the values and try logging in near expiry to see the warning. A common misconception is that chage forces an immediate password change; instead it sets metadata that the system checks at login or at password-change time. Verify your changes by listing the user's aging information and by simulating an upcoming expiry using shorter maximum values in a test environment. This approach separates policy (how often passwords must change) from enforcement of complexity, which remains the role of PAM modules.

keyIdea.title: chage manages expiry
keyIdea.text: Use chage to schedule rotation and warnings, then verify account metadata and user-visible warnings.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Password aging with chage
chage examples
Set maximum age, minimum interval, and warning days for a user.
# Example: set maximum 90 days, minimum 7 days, warn 14 days
chage -M 90 -m 7 -W 14 username

# View aging information
chage -l username
What to verify
  • Run the chage list command to see the updated fields.
  • Confirm that users receive a warning within the configured window before expiry.
  • Use a short max value in a lab to test the expiry workflow quickly.
Scenario and pitfalls
A typical policy sets a maximum and a warning to ensure users rotate credentials without surprises. Avoid setting minimum to zero if you have password-history controls, because users could cycle through weak variants quickly. Also remember chage changes metadata; it does not change password complexity.
Common mistake
Assuming the warning will appear via email. The warning is shown at login or password-change; notify users separately if you need email reminders.
Key Takeaway

Use chage to enforce rotation windows and always validate with the chage list and a user login test to confirm warnings.

screens.title: Sudo and least privilege
screens.subtitle: Grant only the commands required and audit all elevations

narration.text: Sudo allows trusted users to run specific commands as the superuser or another account. The security principle to apply is least privilege: give users only the minimum rights they need to perform tasks. That means avoiding group membership that grants full root powers and preferring explicit command entries in the sudoers file. Use visudo to edit sudoers safely because it performs syntax checks before saving, preventing misformatted rules that could lock out access. For example, if an administrator needs only to restart web services, specify the exact systemctl restart commands for those services rather than giving access to systemctl generally. Always test both an allowed command, which should succeed, and a disallowed command, which should fail with a sudo error. Auditability matters: sudo logs every executed command so you can review who ran what and when in the auth logs or journal. A common mistake is to add NOPASSWD where a password prompt would otherwise add accountability. Another is to assume a command's path is the same on every distribution — prefer absolute paths in sudoers entries. Your verification steps should include checking logs after running a permitted command and confirming denied attempts produce clear failures. This practice reduces accidental or malicious privilege escalation and creates an audit trail for investigations.

keyIdea.title: Least-privilege sudo
keyIdea.text: Use visudo and exact command entries to grant minimal elevated capabilities while preserving audit logs.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Sudo and least privilege
Why scoping sudo matters
A narrowly scoped sudo entry limits what a compromised account can do and makes audits meaningful.
Best practice
Use visudo, prefer command aliases for clarity, and list absolute command paths to avoid ambiguity between distributions.
Audit
Review /var/log/auth.log or journal entries to see who executed an elevated command and when. Sudo creates a reliable trail when used correctly.
Key Takeaway

Restrict sudo to exact commands and verify audit logs after allowing elevated actions to maintain control and visibility.

Analogy & example
Think of sudo entries as giving keys that open only specific doors. Instead of handing someone a master key, grant access to the single service door they need. The code panel on the next slide contains a secure example that grants restart rights for two services without broader control.
Common mistake
Adding a user to the sudo or wheel group without understanding the resulting privileges effectively grants full root access, removing accountability and increasing risk.

screens.title: Sudoers best practices and a visudo example
screens.subtitle: Safe editing, aliases, and a narrow service example

narration.text: Edit the sudoers file only with visudo to prevent syntax errors that can disable administrative access. Use User_Alias and Cmnd_Alias to keep entries readable and maintainable. In a common scenario you may want an operations user to restart specific services but not gain an interactive root shell. The example on this slide shows a compact sudoers snippet that defines a user alias, a command alias for service restarts, and grants the user that alias only as root. After adding the entry, test both the allowed restart command and an attempted shell elevation. The allowed command should run and produce the expected service output. The denied command should fail with a sudo error and be recorded in the auth logs. A practical pitfall is assuming NOPASSWD is harmless; removing the prompt can be convenient but reduces accountability. Also ensure command paths are exact; a different path breaks the rule or can be exploited. Use the audit trail to confirm who executed the permitted actions. This controlled approach keeps elevated privileges focused on tasks, not people. Sudoers best practices and a visudo example means group commands and users with aliases and grant only what is necessary — then test and inspect logs.. In practical terms, safe editing, aliases, and a narrow service example. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: visudo + aliases
keyIdea.text: Group commands and users with aliases and grant only what is necessary — then test and inspect logs.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Sudoers example
Visudo snippet
Define aliases and give the user only the service restart commands needed.
# Sudoers snippet example
User_Alias APACHE_NGINX_ADMINS = opsadmin
Cmnd_Alias SERVICE_RESTARTS = /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx, /usr/bin/systemctl restart apache2
APACHE_NGINX_ADMINS ALL=(root) SERVICE_RESTARTS
Testing
  1. Run an allowed restart command as the opsadmin user and expect success.
  2. Attempt a disallowed command such as opening a shell with sudo; expect denial and a log entry.
Practical notes
  • Prefer absolute paths in Cmnd_Alias to avoid ambiguity.
  • Avoid NOPASSWD unless required and reviewed for accountability impacts.
  • Group similar commands into aliases to make audits and reviews easier.
Common mistake
Using broad wildcards or directories in command lists can unintentionally widen privileges. Be explicit and conservative.

screens.title: System users and non-interactive accounts
screens.subtitle: Why services run as dedicated users and how to audit them

narration.text: Linux distributions create system users to run services with constrained privileges. These accounts — such as daemon, nginx, or mysql — should not allow interactive logins. Typically their shells are set to a non-interactive value and their password field indicates no login. Running services as dedicated, unprivileged users limits the files and capabilities each service can access. For example, a web server running as a dedicated user should own only its web content directories, preventing code execution from escaping into unrelated parts of the system. Auditing system accounts involves inspecting /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow for unexpected interactive shells or non-empty password fields. If you find a system account with a login shell, consider changing it to a non-interactive shell and adjusting file ownership. A common misconception is that services need root to bind low ports or write logs; in many cases they only need specific capabilities or helper utilities at startup and can drop privileges after. When you manage system users, document their purpose and verify they follow least privilege. Regular audits ensure that newly installed packages do not create interactive system users inadvertently and that ownership and permissions remain tight.

keyIdea.title: Use dedicated non-interactive users
keyIdea.text: Run services under limited accounts, restrict shells, and audit account entries regularly for unexpected interactive access.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › System users
What are system users?
Non-interactive accounts created by the OS or packages to run services and limit privileges.
Audit checklist
  • Inspect /etc/passwd for unexpected login shells.
  • Check /etc/shadow for password hashes where system users should be locked.
  • Confirm service files and data directories are owned by the service user and not root.
Example: nginx
Nginx commonly runs as a dedicated nginx user with a non-interactive shell. Grant only read access to web content and restrict write permissions to upload directories that need them. Never run the whole service as root for normal operations.
Common oversight
Installing packages with improper defaults can create system users with interactive shells; include shell and password checks in regular audits.
Key Takeaway

Non-interactive system users reduce risk when services are compromised. Audit and fix shells and ownership to maintain least privilege.

screens.title: Account locking with pam_faillock
screens.subtitle: Block repeated failed attempts and reduce brute-force exposure

narration.text: pam_faillock provides an automatic account lockout mechanism after a configurable number of consecutive authentication failures. Configure it in the auth and account sections of the relevant PAM file for services you wish to protect, such as the sshd stack. Typical options include the number of allowed failures, a short unlock time, and whether to apply locks to root. For example, a deny count of three with an unlock time of ten minutes will make repeated password guessing far less effective. After adding the lines, restart the service that uses the pam. d file and test from a separate client or session so you do not lock yourself out locally. When a lock occurs, faillock records the failure and prevents further attempts until the unlock time expires or an administrator resets the lock. A frequent misconception is that account locking alone is sufficient; pairing it with monitoring such as fail2ban gives both immediate account-level protection and network-level blocking of abusive IP addresses. Verify your configuration by deliberately failing authentication the required number of times, then inspecting faillock output for the user and ensuring the account behaves as expected. Always test on a non-production account or from a different machine to avoid losing administrative access.

keyIdea.title: Lock after failures
keyIdea.text: Use pam_faillock to automatically lock accounts after repeated failures and inspect faillock records to understand attacks.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › pam_faillock configuration
PAM faillock snippet
Place these lines into the auth and account sections of the service's pam.d file, for example sshd.
# auth section (top)
auth    required    pam_faillock.so preauth silent deny=3 unlock_time=600 even_deny_root
auth    [success=1 default=bad] pam_unix.so try_first_pass

# account section (top)
account required    pam_faillock.so
Guidance
  • Use a low deny count and a sensible unlock period to slow brute-force attempts without causing excessive user frustration.
  • Test from a separate client to avoid locking your own session.
Testing and recovery
After triggering a lock, use the faillock utility to display and reset locks for a user. If a legitimate user is locked, an administrator can reset their failures to restore access.
Common mistake
Applying locks without testing from a separate machine can lock out administrators. Always have an alternate session available during changes.
Key Takeaway

pam_faillock offers per-account rate limiting. Combine it with monitoring and network-level blocking to effectively reduce brute-force success rates.

screens.title: fail2ban — dynamic blocking from logs
screens.subtitle: How fail2ban parses logs and updates firewall rules

narration.text: fail2ban is a log-driven intrusion prevention tool that reads system logs to find patterns of abuse, such as repeated failed SSH login attempts, and then temporarily updates firewall rules to block the offending IP addresses. You configure jail rules that specify which log files to scan, the regex patterns to match, and the ban duration. A simple SSH jail will monitor authentication failures, count occurrences from the same IP, and then add a block to iptables or nftables for a configurable period. After deployment, review the fail2ban logs and the active bans to understand the attack surface and tune thresholds. A common mistake is overly aggressive bans that block legitimate users after a few failed attempts, so tune the failure threshold and bantime to balance security and availability. Also be mindful that fail2ban depends on log formats; custom SSH setups that change log messages may require adjusted filters. In lab tests purposely trigger a failed authentication pattern and then confirm the IP appears in fail2ban-client output and in the firewall rules. Combining fail2ban with account-level locks like pam_faillock defends both the account and the network perimeter.

keyIdea.title: Log-driven blocking
keyIdea.text: fail2ban translates log patterns into temporary firewall bans, giving quick automated defense against repetitive attacks.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › fail2ban overview
How fail2ban works
fail2ban monitors logs, matches patterns, and adds temporary bans to the firewall for offending IPs.
Typical configuration elements
  • Jail definition pointing to a log file and filter.
  • Filter regex that matches failure messages.
  • Bantime and maxretry settings to tune sensitivity.
Key Takeaway

Use fail2ban to react quickly to abusive sources by dynamically updating firewall rules, and tune it to avoid blocking legitimate users.

Lab verification
  1. Enable an SSH jail and attempt repeated failed logins from a test IP.
  2. Use the fail2ban client to list jails and show banned IPs.
  3. Confirm the firewall reflects the ban and that bans expire as configured.
Common mistake
Fail2ban relies on expected log formats. If logs are customized or forwarded, filters may miss events and require adjustment.

screens.title: Putting it together — a secure account workflow
screens.subtitle: How PAM, chage, sudo, faillock, and fail2ban interact

narration.text: Secure account management is a layered process: PAM enforces password quality at creation and change time, chage handles expiry and warnings, sudo grants controlled elevation and creates an audit trail, pam_faillock stops repeated guessing at the account level, and fail2ban responds at the network level by blocking abusive IPs. These controls are complementary — PAM enforces what a password must look like, chage ensures passwords rotate, sudo limits what a user can do with privileges, and the locking and banning tools reduce the likelihood that credentials are guessed or used by attackers. In practice you should configure each layer, then validate them together: create a test user, set a strong password that meets PAM rules, set a short expiry and warning, add a narrowly scoped sudoers entry, and from another machine trigger failed authentications to observe faillock and fail2ban behaviors. When tuning, balance security and availability: overly aggressive bans or very short expiry may increase helpdesk load. A common operational mistake is making changes on production without a rollback plan; always test changes in a staging environment and have an out-of-band admin session available during risky edits. The real value is in combining these measures so they reinforce each other and produce both prevention and observability.

keyIdea.title: Layered defenses
keyIdea.text: Combine PAM, chage, sudo, and automated blocking to create prevention, detection, and audit layers for account security.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Secure account workflow
Workflow summary
A concise, repeatable process you can run in a lab or production validation.
Step 1
Enforce PAM
Set pam_pwquality rules for complexity and dictionary checks.
Step 2
Set aging
Use chage for max age, min change interval, and warn days.
Step 3
Scope sudo
Add minimal sudoers entries with visudo and test logs.
Step 4
Lock on failure
Configure pam_faillock to block repeated attempts per account.
Step 5
Block abusive IPs
Deploy fail2ban jails to add temporary firewall bans for noisy attackers.
Key Takeaway

A layered approach gives prevention, detection, and the audit trail you need to investigate incidents and limit damage from compromised credentials.

Check your understanding
Which combination of settings would you adjust first if users complain about frequent lockouts: pam_faillock deny, fail2ban maxretry, or chage warn days? Think about balance.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: These compact cards collect the most important technical concepts from the chapter. First, PAM is the central, modular system that lets you apply consistent authentication rules across services. Second, pam_pwquality enforces complexity requirements and dictionary checks at password creation time, preventing weak credentials from being accepted. Third, chage manages password aging and warnings, ensuring credentials rotate at predictable intervals. Keep these three concepts in mind as you configure systems: PAM enforces what is accepted, pam_pwquality shapes strength, and chage schedules renewals. In practice you will combine them so that only strong, recently rotated passwords are allowed to authenticate. A simple check after each change is to create a test account and exercise creation, change, and expiry behavior to make sure policies behave as expected. These reminders form the basis for safe account management.

keyIdea.title: Remember the trio
keyIdea.text: PAM, pam_pwquality, and chage together control authentication quality and lifecycle.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Key Concepts — Part 1
Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM)
Modular framework that centralizes authentication policy so changes apply across services.
pam_pwquality
Module to enforce password length, class requirements, and dictionary checks during password changes.
chage
Utility to set maximum password age, minimum change interval, and warning windows for accounts.
Summary
Combine quality checks, lifecycle rules, and verification steps to raise and maintain credential hygiene.

narration.text: These three final concept cards capture operational controls you should apply routinely. First, sudo and visudo let you grant and audit elevated commands; prefer exact command entries and aliases for clarity. Second, system users should be non-interactive accounts owned by services, preventing direct logins and limiting file access. Third, combine pam_faillock and fail2ban to stop repeated guessing at both the account and network layers. Together these measures give you least-privilege elevation, reduced attack surface, and automated blocking against noisy attackers. After configuring these controls, run a short verification routine: test sudo entries, check account shells and ownership, and simulate failed logins to confirm locks and bans. Regular audits and conservative defaults are the operational practices that make these controls effective in production environments. Key Concepts — Part 2 means sudo scoping, non-interactive system users, and automated locking form the operational guardrails for safe systems.. In practical terms, operational controls and best practices. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Operational security
keyIdea.text: Sudo scoping, non-interactive system users, and automated locking form the operational guardrails for safe systems.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Key Concepts — Part 2
sudo and visudo
Grant minimal command-level privileges and edit safely with visudo to avoid syntax errors.
System users
Run services as dedicated, non-login accounts and verify ownership and shells in /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow.
pam_faillock & fail2ban
Combine per-account locks with log-driven IP bans to stop both targeted and noisy brute-force attempts.
Final takeaway
Apply configuration, then verify with test users and log checks. Conservative defaults and regular audits keep these controls effective.
